The ending feels completely natural, purposeful, and earned because it directly resolves the central thematic tension established in the first half of the story. Early on, the narrative focuses on the congregation's belief that by moving to the affluent suburbs and building a monumental new synagogue, they had "built an ark of suburban permanence" where "history felt suspended" and "nothing bad could penetrate walls this expensive." Barbara also contemplates the world her unborn child is about to enter. 

After the climax of the shooting shatters this illusion of safety and decorum, the final paragraphs bring these themes full circle. As Barbara stands outside in the cold parking lot, the physical kick of her baby prompts her final realization: "that they had not escaped history after all; they had merely brought it with them." This provides a strong sense of thematic closure and marks the exact emotional and philosophical moment the entire piece was leading readers toward.
